subtitle: Long words from short ones, and -in for a woman
words.intro: The Baumarkt, the German DIY store, is where the long words live: Gartenschlauch, Waschmaschine, Schraubenzieher. Every one of them is two short words you know.

opener.caption: Ein Baumarkt: Schrauben, Nägel, Werkzeug, und ein Schild für alles.
reading.intro: Maya's new room has books on the floor. Lena says: a shelf, a Saturday, a Baumarkt. The Baumarkt has four thousand things and one word for each.
reading.photos[0].caption: Gasflaschen vor dem Baumarkt: Gas + Flasche = Gasflasche.
reading.photos[1].caption: Eine alte Eisenwarenhandlung in Bayern: Eisen + Waren + Handlung. Drei Wörter, ein Laden.
reading.en: Maya: Lena, this is not a shop. This is a city. · Lena: This is a Baumarkt. Bau plus Markt. Everything for the house. What do you need? · Maya: A shelf. For books. A Bücherregal! · Lena: Very good! Bücher plus Regal. And for the shelf you need screws and a screwdriver. · Maya: Schrauben-zieher. The thing pulls the screw? · Lena: Exactly. And for the picture on the wall you need a nail and a hammer. · Maya: Excuse me, where do I find screws? · Assistant: Aisle twelve, on the left. Which size? · Maya: Er. For a bookshelf. · Assistant: Then four by forty. The pack costs two ninety. · Maya: Lena, what is that: Handwerkerin? · Lena: A Handwerker is a man who works with his hands. Handwerkerin is the woman. Today you are a Handwerkerin. · Maya: With a screwdriver and two ninety. Germany is easy.
reading.fact: Germans build a long word instead of a phrase: *Bücherregal*, not “shelf for books”. The longest in everyday use is probably *Kraftfahrzeughaftpflichtversicherung*, car insurance, and even Germans say *KFZ-Versicherung*.

grammar[0].fact: Job adverts in Germany write *Handwerker (m/w/d)*: male, female, diverse. The law has required the third option since 2018.
grammar[1].subheading: Compounds: read from the back, and the last word owns the article
grammar[1].photo.caption: Das Klingelschild: Klingel + Schild. Der Schild? Nein: das Schild, also das Klingelschild.
grammar[1].blocks[0].title: Word + word = new word
grammar[1].blocks[0].note: The last word decides what it is — and its article.
grammar[1].blocks[1].blocks[0].title: Read from the back
grammar[1].blocks[1].blocks[0].text: *Kinderzimmer*: Zimmer (room) … for Kinder. *Haustür*: Tür (door) … of the Haus. Start at the end.
grammar[1].blocks[1].blocks[1].title: You already know one
grammar[1].blocks[1].blocks[1].text: *die Telefonnummer* = das Telefon + die Nummer. Once you know Kuchen, you know Apfelkuchen and Käsekuchen too.
grammar[1].check.title: Mini-Check
grammar[1].fact: The little *-n* or *-s* between two words is the *Fugenelement*, the joint: Schokolade*n*kuchen, Geburtstag*s*kuchen. Germans argue about where it belongs, too.
document.caption: Eine Eisenwarenhandlung in Anzing, Bayern. Wie viele Fenster, wie viele Wörter?
document.intro: An old hardware shop. Count what you see, then take the long word on its sign apart.
document.fact: *Eisenwarenhandlung*: iron + goods + trade, the shop that sold nails before the Baumarkt existed. The small towns still have one, and the owner knows which screw you need.
